title: Where does the log go? How dead things return to the air and the soil

summary.text: A coconut palm falls in a storm, and a few months later the trunk is soft, then crumbly, then gone. Where did it go? You test a jar of soil with limewater and find that the soil breathes out a gas. You chop carrots to see why small pieces rot first, and you grow methi in rotted stuff to see if it feeds a new plant. You learn that matter goes round and round, while energy flows through and leaves as heat. You also meet the vultures of India, and what happened when a painkiller took the cleanup crew away.
summary.art: A fallen coconut palm trunk in a Kerala yard, half soft and covered with mushrooms, with a young banana plant growing beside it.

intro.hook: A big coconut palm falls in a storm. Nobody moves it. Come back in two years, and the trunk is gone. There is no heap of wood and nobody carried it away. Where did all that tree go?
intro.text: A palm trunk weighs more than a hundred kilograms. It cannot just vanish. Some of it went into the soil. Some of it went somewhere you cannot see. In this unit you catch the invisible part in a jar, you find out why small pieces rot faster than big ones, and you grow a plant in rotted leaves to see who gets the rest.
intro.art: A child kneeling by a rotting palm trunk with a notebook, and a mushroom shelf growing out of the wood.

outcomes: I can name three kinds of cleanup crew (scavengers, detritivores and decomposers) and say what each one does.
I can explain that decomposers digest dead things with enzymes and breathe out carbon dioxide, and I can show it with limewater.
I can explain that most of a rotting leaf or log goes back to the air as gas, and the rest becomes soil that feeds new plants.
I can explain the difference between matter, which goes round in a cycle, and energy, which flows through and leaves as heat.
I can predict how fast something will rot from its size, warmth, water and air, and test my prediction with a fair test.
I can explain what goes wrong when a cleanup crew is missing, using a real example.
I can design and test a way to speed up or slow down rotting, changing one thing at a time.

terms.meaning: A living being, such as a fungus or a bacterium, who feeds on dead things by digesting them and soaking up the food.
terms.example: The white threads of a mould growing through a fallen branch are decomposers at work.
terms.art: A fallen branch with white fungus threads spreading through the wood.

terms.meaning: An animal who eats bits of dead plants and animals and breaks them into smaller pieces. Detritus is the word for dead bits.
terms.example: An earthworm pulls a dead leaf into the soil and eats it. A millipede and a woodlouse do the same.
terms.art: An earthworm dragging a dead leaf into a hole in the soil.

terms.meaning: An animal who finds and eats dead animals, or leftover food, that she did not kill herself.
terms.example: A vulture eats a dead cow. A crow picks at rice dropped on the road.
terms.art: A vulture on a fence post and a crow beside a dropped heap of rice.

terms.meaning: A tiny tool made by a living being that cuts food into pieces small enough to soak up.
terms.example: A mould pours enzymes onto a piece of bread, and the bread softens as it is cut up.
terms.art: A drawing of a mould thread dripping tiny scissors onto a piece of bread.

terms.meaning: The way every living being gets energy from food. The food is broken down using oxygen, and carbon dioxide and water come out.
terms.example: You breathe out carbon dioxide because your cells are doing respiration. Soil microbes do the same.
terms.art: A child and a clump of soil each breathing out small bubbles labelled carbon dioxide.

terms.meaning: A gas with no colour or smell. It is made when living things get energy from food, and when things burn. Plants take it in to make food.
terms.example: Limewater turns milky when carbon dioxide mixes with it.
terms.art: A glass of limewater half clear and half milky, with bubbles rising through it.

terms.meaning: The simple materials, such as nitrogen and phosphorus, that plants soak up from the soil with water and use to build their bodies.
terms.example: Rotted leaves release nutrients into the soil, and the next plant's roots drink them in.
terms.art: Plant roots reaching towards glowing dots in dark soil, labelled nutrients.

terms.meaning: The dark, soft, crumbly part of the soil that is left when dead plants and animals have been partly broken down.
terms.example: The black crumbly soil under a heap of old leaves is rich in humus.
terms.art: A spadeful of dark crumbly soil held in two hands.

terms.meaning: The layer of fallen leaves, twigs and other dead bits that covers the ground under trees.
terms.example: In a forest, the leaf litter is full of millipedes, beetles, worms and fungus threads.
terms.art: The floor of a forest covered with leaves, with tiny creatures moving among them.

terms.meaning: The outside of a thing, where it meets the air, the water or other living things. Cutting a thing up makes more surface.
terms.example: A grated carrot has far more surface than a whole carrot of the same weight.
terms.art: A whole carrot beside a heap of grated carrot with the cut faces drawn in red.

terms.meaning: The path that the same atoms follow round and round, from the air to a plant, to an animal or a decomposer, and back to the air or soil.
terms.example: A carbon atom in your breath may become part of a leaf, then a caterpillar, then the soil, then the air again.
terms.art: A circle of arrows joining air, a plant, an animal, a decomposer and the soil.

terms.meaning: The one-way path of energy through living things. It comes from the Sun, passes along food chains, and ends as heat that spreads out and is not used again.
terms.example: The warmth of a compost heap is energy from sunlight, once stored in leaves, now leaving as heat.
terms.art: A long arrow from the Sun through a leaf, a goat and a mushroom, ending in wavy heat lines.

explanations.concept: Three cleanup crews: scavengers, detritivores and decomposers
explanations.definition: Dead things are cleared by three crews. Scavengers eat whole dead animals and leftovers. Detritivores chew dead plants and animals into small bits. Decomposers, mainly fungi and bacteria, digest the bits with enzymes and soak up the food.
explanations.description: Each crew does a different job, and they work in order. A dead cow is found first by vultures and crows, who are scavengers. Flies lay eggs on what is left, and the grubs eat the soft parts. Then beetles and other small animals chew the rest into bits. A dead leaf follows the same order. A millipede or an earthworm is a detritivore. She chews the leaf, and the bits she leaves behind are small. Fungi and bacteria then cover those small bits, pour enzymes on them and soak up the food. The three crews need each other. Without detritivores, decomposers have only the outside of a big leaf to work on. Without decomposers, the bits of leaf would pile up. No crew is the boss. Together they turn a dead body back into soil and air.
examples: Vultures and crows clear a dead animal first, and are scavengers.
Earthworms, millipedes, woodlice, termites and dung beetles chew dead things small, and are detritivores.
Moulds, mushrooms and soil bacteria digest the small bits, and are decomposers.
explanations.art: A dead leaf passing through three scenes: a millipede chewing it, then fungus threads covering the bits, then dark soil.

explanations.concept: Rotting is a slow, cool kind of burning
explanations.definition: Decomposers get energy from dead food by respiration. They use oxygen to break the food down, and they give out carbon dioxide, water and a little heat. A fire does the same thing quickly and hot.
explanations.description: When wood burns, the carbon in the wood joins with oxygen from the air and becomes carbon dioxide. The energy comes out as heat and light. When a fungus eats wood, the same thing happens, only slowly. The fungus pours enzymes on the wood and soaks up the sugars. Inside her body, she joins the sugars with oxygen and gets energy. Carbon dioxide and water leave. So a rotting log is breathing out, all the time, into the air. This is why a jar of damp soil with a little peel turns limewater milky. The soil is breathing. A big pile of rotting leaves can even feel warm, because all that tiny breathing gives out heat. Burning and rotting turn the same dead plant into the same gases. One takes minutes. The other takes years.
examples: Limewater above damp soil turns milky, because soil microbes breathe out carbon dioxide.
A heap of wet grass cuttings feels warm in the middle, from the heat of respiration.
A candle, a fire and a rotting log all join carbon with oxygen to make carbon dioxide.
explanations.art: A burning log and a rotting log side by side, each with arrows showing oxygen going in and carbon dioxide and heat coming out.

explanations.concept: Where does the log go? Mostly into the air
explanations.definition: When a dead plant is decomposed, a large share of its carbon is breathed out by the decomposers as carbon dioxide. The rest becomes the bodies of decomposers, humus in the soil, and nutrients taken up by new plants.
explanations.description: A tree builds its wood mostly from carbon dioxide taken from the air, as you learned in the photosynthesis unit. So when the wood rots, much of it goes back the way it came. Decomposers breathe out the carbon as carbon dioxide, and the rest of the matter leaves as water vapour. In many studies of fallen leaves in warm, wet places, a large share of the carbon is breathed out within a year or two. What stays behind is partly the bodies of the fungi and bacteria, and partly dark, crumbly humus. The minerals in the wood, such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, dissolve in rain and sink into the soil. A root can then drink them. So the tree does not disappear. Part goes up into the air, part goes down into the soil, and plants take both back again.
examples: A rotting palm trunk loses weight mostly as carbon dioxide and water vapour.
A compost heap shrinks to a small fraction of the weight of the kitchen scraps that went in.
Banana plants beside a rotting trunk grow with the minerals it releases.
explanations.art: A rotting log with one arrow going up to the air labelled carbon dioxide, and another going down into soil labelled minerals and humus.

explanations.concept: Matter goes round, energy goes through
explanations.definition: The atoms in living things are used again and again, so matter moves in cycles. Energy is not used again. It comes from the Sun, passes along food chains, and leaves as heat.
explanations.description: Earth gets very few new atoms. The carbon in your body has been in plants, animals and the air before. A decomposer does not make new carbon. She only moves it on. Energy is different. A leaf holds energy from sunlight. A caterpillar eats the leaf and uses the energy to move and grow, and some leaves as heat. A fungus eats the caterpillar's droppings and the rest of the energy leaves as heat. Heat spreads into the air and into space, and no living thing can use it again. So life on Earth stays alive because the Sun keeps sending new energy, while the atoms keep going round. Decomposers are where the loop closes: they send the atoms back so plants can start again.
examples: The same carbon atoms pass from air to leaf to caterpillar to soil and back to air.
The Sun's energy passes along the food chain and ends as heat. It does not go back to the leaf.
A compost heap stays warm for weeks because stored energy is leaving as heat.
explanations.art: A circle of arrows for atoms going round, and a straight arrow from the Sun to a wavy line of heat for energy passing through.

explanations.concept: Why small pieces rot faster: decomposers work on surfaces
explanations.definition: Decomposers can only work on the outside of their food. The more surface a food has, the more room they have to work, so small pieces rot faster than big pieces of the same weight.
explanations.description: A fungus cannot go inside a solid lump. She pours enzymes on the outside and soaks up what dissolves. A whole carrot has a small outside. Cut it into small cubes, and every cut makes new surface. A cube 4 centimetres on each side has a surface of 96 square centimetres. Cut it into 64 cubes of 1 centimetre, and the surface becomes 384 square centimetres. It is four times as much, with the same amount of carrot. This is why earthworms, millipedes and termites matter. They chew leaves into bits, and every bit gives fungi and bacteria new surface to work on. It is also why we chop vegetables for compost, and why a pile of whole logs takes much longer to rot than a pile of sawdust.
examples: Grated carrot rots in a few days. A whole carrot lasts weeks.
Sawdust rots much faster than a log of the same weight.
Worms and millipedes speed up rotting by shredding leaves.
explanations.art: A big cube cut into 64 small cubes, with the new cut faces drawn in colour.

explanations.concept: How dead things feed the next plant
explanations.definition: Decomposers release the minerals locked in dead things into the soil water. Plant roots drink these nutrients and use them to build new leaves, stems and seeds.
explanations.description: A dead leaf contains nitrogen in its proteins. Soil bacteria and fungi break the proteins apart and release the nitrogen as ammonium. Other soil bacteria change ammonium into nitrate, which dissolves in water, and a root can soak it up. Phosphorus and potassium are released in a similar way. This is why a rotted heap makes a rich soil, and why a farm field needs nutrients put back when the crop is carried away and not left to rot. It is also why the nutrients in many tropical rainforests are mostly held in the living trees. The soil is often poor, but the leaf litter rots so fast in the warm, wet air that the nutrients go straight back into roots. If the forest is cleared, the nutrients are lost.
examples: Methi seeds grow greener in soil with rotted compost than in plain cocopeat.
Farmers put back dung and crop leftovers so the soil keeps its nutrients.
A rainforest recycles its nutrients so fast that the soil below can look poor.
explanations.art: Dead leaves above soil, with arrows showing the nutrients going down and a new plant's roots taking them up.

explanations.concept: Fast and slow cycles: heat, water and air decide
explanations.definition: Decomposers work fastest when it is warm, wet and airy. They work slowly when it is cold, dry or flooded with no air. So the same leaf can rot in months in one place and last thousands of years in another.
explanations.description: In a warm, wet forest, such as the Western Ghats in the monsoon, a fallen leaf may be mostly gone within a few months. In a cold northern forest, it can take years. In a peat bog, the ground is full of water and has almost no air, so most decomposers cannot breathe. Dead plants pile up there. Over thousands of years they turn into peat, and over millions of years, when buried deep, peat can turn into coal. In a desert, there is too little water, so a dry dead branch can stay for decades. That is why a desert and a bog both keep old things safe. Rotting is not a clock that ticks the same everywhere. It is a living process, and it runs on warmth, water and air.
examples: A leaf in a warm, wet forest rots in months, and the same leaf in a cold forest can take years.
A peat bog preserves plants for thousands of years because there is almost no air.
A dry wooden door frame in a desert can last for decades.
explanations.art: Three scenes side by side: a warm wet forest floor with a thin leaf layer, a cold forest with a thick layer, and a bog with dark peat.

explanations.concept: Termites and fungus farms: decomposers work in teams
explanations.definition: Many decomposers work in partnership. Some termites keep microbes in their guts that digest wood. Other termites grow gardens of fungus, feed it on chewed plants, and eat the fungus.
explanations.description: Wood is hard to digest, because it is made of tough fibres. No termite makes the right enzymes for all of it. Some kinds of termites carry tiny microbes in their guts that do the work. In India, the termites called Odontotermes build tall mounds and keep a fungus garden inside. The workers bring chewed plants, the fungus, called Termitomyces, grows on them, and the termites eat the fungus. In the rainy season, the fungus sends up mushrooms from the mound or the ground close by. People in many parts of India collect and eat these mushrooms. In both cases, the partnership digests what neither partner could digest alone.
examples: A termite is a detritivore with decomposers living in her gut.
Odontotermes termites grow a fungus garden inside their mound.
Termite mushrooms are collected and eaten in the rainy season in several states of India.
explanations.art: A cutaway of a termite mound showing chewed plant bits, a grey fungus garden and workers tending it.

explanations.concept: When the cleanup crew is missing
explanations.definition: Dead bodies and dung get cleared by a crew of scavengers and detritivores that have been fitted to the job for millions of years. If the crew is removed, or if new things arrive that the crew cannot eat, the leftovers pile up.
explanations.description: By the 1960s, Australia had millions of cattle, and they produced huge amounts of dung. The local dung beetles were fitted to the dry pellets of kangaroos and could not use it, so the dung dried into hard pads that covered the grass and bred flies. The scientist George Bornemissza brought in dung beetles from Africa and Europe to bury it. In India, in the 1990s and 2000s, more than 95 of every 100 vultures of three kinds died after eating cattle treated with the painkiller diclofenac. Carcasses lay longer in the open. Scientists agree that the loss of vultures changed how dead cattle were cleared. They disagree about how much it raised the number of street dogs and the risk of rabies. And plastic is a third case: it is so new that almost no decomposer can eat it yet.
examples: Australian cattle dung piled up until African and European dung beetles were brought in.
Vultures in India crashed by more than 95 percent in about ten years.
Plastic bags stay for hundreds of years because few microbes can digest them.
explanations.art: A field with a dead cow, an empty sky, and a pack of street dogs gathering where vultures used to circle.

perspectives.explanation: With fewer vultures, more dead cattle were left for street dogs. Dog numbers went up, and researchers estimated more dog bites and more risk of rabies in people.
Dog numbers also depend on food waste, vaccination and many other things. It is hard to show how much of any rise in rabies came from the loss of vultures alone.

agreed.text: Fungi and bacteria digest dead plants and animals with enzymes, and give out carbon dioxide, water and heat.
agreed.evidence: Soil, leaf litter and compost heaps give off carbon dioxide that can be measured, and compost heaps warm up.

agreed.text: Most of the carbon in a rotting log or leaf goes back to the air as carbon dioxide.
agreed.evidence: Scientists measure the carbon dioxide leaving the soil and the weight lost by leaves in mesh bags left on forest floors.

agreed.text: Matter cycles on Earth, while energy flows through living things and ends as heat.
agreed.evidence: The atoms in a food chain can be tracked from plants to animals to soil, and the heat given off at each step can be measured.

agreed.text: Warm, wet, airy places rot things fastest. Cold, dry or waterlogged places rot things slowly.
agreed.evidence: Leaf bags buried in different climates lose weight at different speeds, and peat bogs preserve plants for thousands of years.

agreed.text: Breaking a food into smaller pieces makes it rot faster.
agreed.evidence: Chopped and ground plant material loses weight faster than whole pieces in the same conditions.

agreed.text: Plastics decompose extremely slowly, because few microbes make enzymes that fit them.
agreed.evidence: Plastic in soil and water is found decades later. A few microbes, such as Ideonella sakaiensis found in Japan in 2016, can digest one kind of plastic, PET, but slowly.

challenging.claim: When something rots, it simply goes away.
challenging.who: Many people, and many young children.
challenging.for: A heap of leaves does shrink, and a banana peel does become a thin brown smear.
challenging.against: Nothing is destroyed. Most of the matter goes into the air as carbon dioxide and water vapour. The rest becomes humus and nutrients in the soil, and the bodies of the decomposers.

challenging.claim: Lush forests must grow on rich soil.
challenging.who: A common idea, from the look of the trees.
challenging.for: A thick, green forest looks as if it must be well fed.
challenging.against: Many tropical rainforests grow on poor soil. Their nutrients are held mostly in the living trees and the fast-rotting leaf litter. When the forest is cleared, the nutrients wash away and the soil turns poor.

challenging.claim: Coal exists because fungi had not yet learned to digest wood.
challenging.who: Floudas and colleagues, in the journal Science, 2012.
challenging.for: Coal came mostly from plants that lived about 300 million years ago. Their study found that fungi able to digest lignin, the toughest part of wood, appeared around that time, and coal formation fell afterwards.
challenging.against: Other scientists point out that coal stopped forming for other reasons too, including changes in climate and the shape of the continents. The question is still being tested.

challenging.claim: Bioplastics that are labelled biodegradable will rot like a banana peel anywhere.
challenging.for: Some plastics are made from plants such as corn, and can be digested.
challenging.against: Many need the steady heat of an industrial compost plant, about 58 degrees Celsius. In a garden, a river or the sea, they can last for years.

challenging.claim: Vultures, hyenas and flies are dirty, and the world is better without them.
challenging.for: They eat rotten meat and carry germs on their bodies.
challenging.against: They are the first crew in the cleanup. When India lost most of its vultures, carcasses lay in the open for longer. Scientists link the loss to more feral dogs, though they disagree about how much.

big_questions.q: Nothing in a forest is called waste, but a city makes a lot of it. What does a forest do with its leftovers that a city does not?
big_questions.hint: Think about who is waiting to eat each leftover.

big_questions.q: The smell of rot makes you hold your nose. To a carrion fly or a dung beetle, it is the smell of dinner. Is the smell in the rotting thing, or in the nose that smells it? Are we smelling differently, or smelling different things?
big_questions.hint: Think about the fruit that a bee sees as ultraviolet and you see as red.

big_questions.q: The carbon in your last breath may once have been in a leaf, a log, or a dinosaur. In what way is it yours?
big_questions.hint: Think about how long you hold on to the atoms of your body.

big_questions.q: Energy goes through living things once and ends as heat. How can life keep going for billions of years if energy is not used again?
big_questions.hint: Where does the next supply of energy come from?

big_questions.q: Plastic stays because nothing has learned to eat it yet. Will something learn? What would that mean?
big_questions.hint: Think about how long leaves have been around, and how long plastic has.

big_questions.q: A mushroom is only the fruit of a fungus. The rest of the fungus is a net of threads in the soil, and in Oregon one such net covers nearly ten square kilometres. Where does one fungus end?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you would count as one living being.

big_questions.q: A tall tree in a rainforest grows in poor soil. Where does her food come from?
big_questions.hint: Think about what lands on the ground every day.

big_questions.q: Every atom in your body was once part of something else. Does that make you new, or old?
big_questions.hint: Think about how long the atoms have been around, and how long you have.

story.title: The Palm That Stayed
story.note: A made-up story. The science in it is real. A fallen trunk is eaten by termites, grubs and fungi. Most of its matter goes into the air as gas, and the rest goes into the soil, where other plants use it.
text: The storm came on the first night of the monsoon. By morning, the yard in Alappuzha was full of torn leaves, and the tall coconut palm by the gate was lying across the path. Meenakshi's grandfather stood over it with his hands on his hips. He did not say anything for a long time.

He had planted that palm the day Meenakshi's mother was born. Thirty-six years she had given coconuts, shade and a place for the crows to quarrel. Now it was a long grey log with a crown of broken fronds.
"I will get Raju to cut it up," said Appooppan. "We can burn the pieces. A dead tree is only a dead tree."

Meenakshi was nine, and she had a notebook with a green cover. She looked at the trunk. It was as thick as her waist and very hard. "Can we wait?" she asked. "Just until Onam. I want to see what happens to it."
"Nothing happens to a log," said Appooppan. But Ammoomma, from the kitchen door, said, "Let the child look." So they made a bargain. The log would stay until Onam.
On the first day, Meenakshi drew the trunk and pushed a thin stick into the bark. It went in the width of her thumbnail. She wrote: "Hard. Ants on the cut end."

After two weeks of rain, the stick went in as far as her first finger joint. The bark had gone dark and damp. Under it she found a thin white web, like cotton thread. She also found a fat, cream-coloured grub, curled up like a comma. A line of mud tubes ran up the side of the trunk, where termites were walking inside, out of the light. She wrote: "The log is full of people."
"Of course it is," said Ammoomma, bringing her a glass of buttermilk. "Everything dead is somebody's dinner."

By the fifth week, the stick slid in as far as her wrist. The cut end of the trunk had turned soft and brown, and orange shelves, like little ears, grew out of the bark. The air near the log smelled of wet earth. A small toad had moved in beneath it. Meenakshi dug out a handful of the wood, and it crumbled in her fingers like a stale biscuit.
She weighed it on the kitchen scale. Then she dried it in the sun for a day and weighed it again. The wood was light. "It is hardly there," she said to herself. "But where did the heavy part go?"
She asked Ammoomma, and Ammoomma only smiled. "What do you think? You were the one who said you wanted to see."

That night, Meenakshi lay awake with the rain on the roof. She thought of the grub chewing, and the white threads, and the mushrooms. All of them were breathing. She remembered a jar from school, where a spoon of soil had turned clear water milky. Maybe the heavy part had gone into the air, a little at a time, through all those tiny breaths.

The week before Onam, Appooppan came out with a cup of tea and found her sitting beside the log. He was grumbling about his banana plants. "The soil is tired," he said. "Every year the bunches get smaller, and every year I buy more fertiliser."

Meenakshi looked at the banana clump next to the log. Then she looked at the other clump, near the well. The leaves beside the log were as wide as umbrellas and dark green. The leaves by the well were pale and thin.

"Appooppan," she said. "Come and look." She pushed the spade into the ground under the old trunk. The earth there was black and crumbly, and full of white threads and small worms. It smelled sweet. She took a handful to him.
He rubbed it between his fingers for a long time. "This is better soil than I have anywhere in the yard," he said.

"It is the palm," said Meenakshi. "It did not go away. Some of it went up into the air, a little at a time, because the grubs and the fungus were breathing it out. The rest went down into the soil. The banana roots found it."
Appooppan looked at the log, and at the banana leaves, and at his granddaughter. "So it is not gone," he said slowly. "It has moved."
"The air part will come back too," said Meenakshi. "The leaves take it in."

He laughed, which he had not done since the storm. He did not call Raju. When Onam came, the log stayed, and a year later, a small coconut seedling pushed up through the soft wood where the trunk had been. Appooppan watered the seedling every morning, and showed everyone who visited where the old palm had gone.
story.epiphany: A dead trunk is not lost. Most of it goes into the air as gas, a little at a time, and the rest goes into the soil, where other plants use it.

items.f: A dung beetle rolls a ball of cow dung and buries it.
items.b: Shredder (detritivore). Dung beetles break up dung and bury it.

items.f: A street dog finds the bones of a goat.
items.b: Scavenger. Dogs eat the leftovers of dead animals.

items.f: Mushrooms grow in a ring on a rotting log.
items.b: Digester (decomposer). The mushrooms are the fruits of a fungus that is digesting the log.

items.f: A woodlouse (pill bug) crunches a dead leaf under a stone.
items.b: Shredder (detritivore). Woodlice eat dead plant matter and make it smaller.

items.f: A styrofoam cup is dropped on a beach.
items.b: Nobody yet. Foam breaks into tiny pieces but few microbes digest it.

items.f: A banana peel turns black on the road after rain.
items.b: Digester (decomposer). Bacteria and yeasts digest the sugars in the peel.

items.f: A line of ants carries away a dead beetle.
items.b: Scavenger. Ants find and carry off dead animals.

items.f: A snail grazes on fallen fruit under a mango tree.
items.b: Shredder (detritivore). She eats the rotting fruit and scrapes it into smaller bits.

items.f: A cotton cloth is buried in damp soil for six months.
items.b: Digester (decomposer). Microbes digest the cotton, because it comes from a plant.

items.f: Maggots eat the soft parts of a dead rat.
items.b: Scavenger. Fly grubs eat dead animals and leave the tougher parts for others.

items.f: A steel spoon is left in damp soil for ten years.
items.b: Nobody yet. A steel spoon rusts, but no decomposer can eat steel.

items.f: A pile of dead leaves in the monsoon turns dark and crumbly.
items.b: Digester (decomposer). Fungi and bacteria work fast when it is warm and wet.

items.f: A crow picks the grains from a dropped heap of rice.
items.b: Scavenger. She eats leftover food before it rots.

items.f: Springtails (tiny jumping insects) eat the fungus threads on a log.
items.b: Shredder (detritivore). Springtails nibble at fungus and dead bits and break them up.

printables.title: 8 tokens: two that say Scavenger, two that say Shredder, two that say Digester and two that say Nobody yet

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not show the back.
Every other player puts one token face down. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader reads the back. Every player whose token matches the first word of the back scores one point.
A player who also says why, in a reason that matches the back, scores one more point. The reader decides, using the back of the card.
With two players, the parent and the child swap roles after every card. A player alone reads the front, picks a token, then turns the card and scores one point for each right answer.
After each card, the reader's job passes to the player on the left.
The game ends when all 24 cards have been read. The player with the most points wins. If there is a tie, the tied players share the win.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the 8 tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile. Give each player one token of each kind.
flow.say: These cards show dead things or leftovers. Each player gets four tokens: Scavenger, Shredder, Digester and Nobody yet. We will guess who comes to eat each thing.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take four tokens.
flow.parent: Fold each card down the middle so the front is on one side and the back on the other, or glue the sheets back to back. A Scavenger finds dead animals and eats them. A Shredder chews dead things small. A Digester pours on enzymes. Nobody yet means no cleanup crew can eat it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Cleanup Crew. You set up the cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Play the game with the rules. The reader reads a card. The others pick a token. Turn over the tokens together and read the back. Ask for a reason each time.
flow.say: Read the front of the card. Do not show the back. Everyone, pick a token. Why did you pick that one? Then I will read the back.
flow.kid: Read a card. Everyone picks a token. Say why. Then check the back.

good: Microbes do not have enzymes that fit it.
It is too new for any decomposer.

ask.q: Why is a termite a Shredder, even though microbes help her?
good: She is an animal who eats dead things.

flow.parent: Stop and talk about any card that is hard. A termite is a Shredder (detritivore) who also has microbes in her gut, so the card makes a good talking point. Keep the score light. Learning from the backs is the point.

check.q: A fungus pours enzymes on a fallen branch and soaks up the food. Which crew is she?
options: Digester (decomposer)
Scavenger
Shredder (detritivore)
check.why: A decomposer digests food outside her body with enzymes. A shredder chews food small, inside her mouth. A scavenger finds dead animals. A wrong pick often comes from thinking that anything which eats a dead thing is a scavenger.

flow.context: In this step, you play the game to the end and learn from each back.

flow.do: Count the scores. Ask your child which crew they found hardest to spot, and which cards surprised them.
flow.say: Which card surprised you most? Which crew was hardest to tell apart? Why?
flow.kid: Which card surprised you most? Which crew was hardest?
flow.parent: The 'Nobody yet' cards are plastic, glass, foam and steel. They are things people made or things nature has not made in the last few million years.
flow.think: Which cards have 'Nobody yet'? What do they have in common?
flow.context: This is the last step of Cleanup Crew. You think back over the game.

experiments.title: The Breathing Soil: what comes out of a jar of soil?
experiments.question: Does damp soil with a little peel give out carbon dioxide? Does warmth change how much?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Jar A has soil and peel in a warm room. Jar B has the same, but sits in the fridge. Jar C has only air. After a day, which limewater will turn milky, and which will stay clear? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Jars A and B have the same soil, the same peel, the same water and the same limewater. Only the place changes: a warm room for A and a fridge for B. Jar C has only air and limewater, so it shows what limewater does with no soil at all.
results_table: What is in it and where it sits

materials.item: 3 clean glass jars with lids, about 500 millilitres each, such as jam or pickle jars
3 small steel katoris or small cups that stand inside a jar
edible chuna, the white lime paste sold at paan shops
soil from a healthy potted plant, or nursery potting soil, about 8 tablespoons
a few finely chopped vegetable peels, such as carrot or banana, about 2 tablespoons
a jug with 1 litre of tap water, a spoon, a drinking straw and a clear glass
a marker, a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Chuna can burn skin and eyes. Only a grown-up handles it. Never taste chuna or limewater. If any splashes in an eye, rinse with plenty of clean water for several minutes and call a doctor. Blow out through the straw only, never suck. Keep jar B sealed, labelled, and on a separate fridge shelf away from food. Wash hands after touching soil and jars. Open the jars outdoors or near a window, because they may smell, and do not put your nose inside.
experiments.record: Draw the three jars. Write the colour of the limewater in each katori after 1 day and after 2 days. Mark which jar sat in the fridge.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you find out what a jar of damp soil gives out. You use limewater, which turns milky when carbon dioxide is added.

setup.art: A jug of water with a teaspoon of white chuna stirred in, and white powder settling at the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. Stir chuna into water and let it settle. The clear water on top is limewater.

setup.art: Three glass jars in a row on a kitchen counter, the first two with soil and peel and the third empty.
setup.caption: 2. Put soil and chopped peel in jars A and B. Leave jar C with only air.

setup.art: A steel katori of clear liquid standing on the soil inside a jar, with the lid beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Stand a katori of clear limewater in each jar. Close the lids.

setup.art: Two jars on a kitchen shelf and one jar on a fridge shelf, each labelled A, C and B.
setup.caption: 4. Jar A and jar C stay on a shelf. Jar B goes in the fridge.

setup.art: Three katoris of limewater side by side, one milky, one a little cloudy and one clear.
setup.caption: 5. After a day, look at the limewater in each katori.

flow.do: Show your child the three jars and the chuna. Say that limewater turns milky when carbon dioxide is added. Ask for a guess and a reason for each jar. Write them down.
flow.say: We will set up three jars. Jar A has soil and peel, and stays in the warm room. Jar B has the same, but goes in the fridge. Jar C has only air. Which limewater will turn milky? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three jars. Which limewater will turn milky? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Which jar do you think will turn the limewater milky first, and why?
good: Jar A, because the soil has living things in it.
Jar A, because it is warm.
None, because soil does not make gas.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write the guesses on the results table. Your child met limewater in the animal breathing unit, if you have done it. If not, a quick breath test through a straw will show it in step 3.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Breathing Soil test. You guess before you set up.

flow.do: A grown-up stirs one level teaspoon of edible chuna into a jug of tap water. Stir for a minute. Cover the jug and leave it for at least one hour.
flow.say: A grown-up does this step. Stir the chuna into the water. Then leave it alone. The white powder will sink to the bottom, and clear water will be left on top.
flow.kid: A grown-up stirs chuna into water. Wait one hour for the powder to sink.
flow.parent: Edible chuna is calcium hydroxide. The clear water on top is limewater. If the water is still cloudy after an hour, wait a little longer. For the best result, make it the evening before. Keep the jug covered, because room air slowly turns the top of the limewater milky.
flow.context: In this step, you make limewater from chuna. It needs time to settle.

flow.do: Label the jars A, B and C. Put 4 tablespoons of soil into jar A and jar B. Add 1 tablespoon of finely chopped peel to each, and sprinkle on 1 tablespoon of water. Leave jar C with only air.
flow.say: Put soil in jars A and B. Add the chopped peel and a spoon of water. Do not put anything in jar C. It is our check on what the limewater does with only air.
flow.kid: Put soil and peel in jars A and B. Jar C stays empty.

ask.q: Why does jar C have no soil in it?
good: It shows what happens with only air.
So we know the milky colour comes from the soil.

flow.parent: Chop the peel as fine as you can, because small pieces rot faster. Do not pack the soil down. The soil needs to be damp but not muddy. The jars will smell a little sweet and sour in a day. That is normal.

check.q: Why do we keep jar C with only air?
options: To see what limewater does with no soil at all
Because we ran out of soil
To make the other jars look better
check.why: A check jar shows what happens without the thing you are testing. If jar C also turned milky, the milky colour could come from the air or the limewater, and not from the soil.

flow.context: In this step, you set up the soil and peel in two of the jars.

flow.do: Pour a little limewater into a clear glass. Blow into it through a straw. It should turn milky. If it does, pour 2 tablespoons of clear limewater into each katori. Stand one katori in each jar and close the lids at once. Put jar B in the fridge.
flow.say: First check your limewater by blowing through a straw. If it turns milky, it works. Then fill the three katoris, stand one in each jar, and close the lids quickly. Jar B goes in the fridge.
flow.kid: Blow into the limewater. It turns milky. Fill three katoris, put one in each jar, close the lids.
flow.parent: Do not let the limewater touch the soil. Keep the powder at the bottom of the jug and pour only the clear water. If the breath test does not turn milky, the chuna may be old. Make a new jug, using a bigger spoon. Put jars A and C in a warm spot out of the sun, such as a kitchen shelf. If your room is cold, jar A may be slow.
flow.context: In this step, you check the limewater, and then seal a katori of it into each jar.

flow.do: The next day, look at the limewater in each katori without opening the jar, if you can see in. Then a grown-up lifts out each katori, one at a time, and you look at the limewater in good light. Write what you see. Look again the day after.
flow.say: Look at each katori. Is the limewater clear, a little cloudy, or milky? Write it down. Then tell me what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Look at each katori. Write clear, cloudy or milky. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.

ask.q: What gas do you think made the limewater milky? Where did it come from?
good: From the soil and the peel.
Something in the soil was breathing.

flow.parent: Expected: jar A is milky within a day, and jar C stays clear, apart from a faint skin on top. Jar B is usually less milky than A, or turns milky later. If jar A is still clear after 2 days, add another tablespoon of chopped peel and a spoon of water, move it somewhere warmer, and look again in a day. Do not explain yet. Let your child say what they saw. Then explain: tiny living things in the soil, the decomposers, eat the peel and breathe out carbon dioxide. The cold slows them down.
flow.think: If the soil is breathing, where does the peel's carbon go?

check.q: Jar A turned milky and jar C stayed clear. What does this show?
options: The soil and peel gave out carbon dioxide
The jar was dirty
Limewater turns milky when it gets old
check.why: Jar C was the check. With only air, the limewater stayed clear. So the gas came from the soil and the peel. A wrong pick often means the check jar was not looked at. Compare the jars side by side.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Breathing Soil test. You read the results and explain them.

schedule.what: Guess. Make the limewater. Set up the three jars and seal the katoris in.
Look at the limewater in each katori. Write the results and explain them. Look once more on day 3 if the colours are unclear.

experiments.title: Cut It Up: does chopping help the decomposers?
experiments.question: A whole carrot, chopped carrot and grated carrot weigh the same. Which one will rot first?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which piece will go soft, smell, or grow mould first: the whole piece, the chopped pieces, or the grated carrot? Which will last longest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All three portions come from the same carrot, so they weigh the same. Each goes in the same kind of box with the same damp tissue, on the same shelf. Only the size of the pieces changes, so any difference comes from the size.

materials.item: 1 big, fresh carrot, about 150 grams
3 clear plastic boxes with lids, or 3 clear zip bags
3 pieces of kitchen tissue
a knife and a grater, and a chopping board (a grown-up cuts)
a spoon of water and a marker
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up uses the knife and the grater. Do not open the boxes once they have fuzzy mould on them, because the spores can make some people sneeze or cough. Look through the clear lid. A grown-up wraps the boxes in a bag and puts them in the bin when the test is over. Wash hands after.
experiments.record: Each day, give each box a score: 0 for no change, 1 for a smell or a soft spot, 2 for slime or a little fuzz, 3 for mostly soft and fuzzy. Write the scores in the table. Draw a line for each carrot over the six days.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you cut one carrot in three ways and watch which part rots first. It tests whether small pieces rot faster than big ones.

setup.art: A carrot cut into three equal lengths on a chopping board, with a knife beside it.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts the carrot into three equal parts by length.

setup.art: Three portions of carrot on a board: one whole piece, one heap of small cubes and one heap of grated carrot.
setup.caption: 2. Leave one part whole. Chop one into small cubes. Grate one.

setup.art: Three clear boxes in a row, each with a damp tissue and a portion of carrot, labelled whole, chopped and grated.
setup.caption: 3. Put each portion on damp tissue in its own box. Close the lids.

setup.art: Three boxes on a kitchen shelf with a notebook and pencil beside them.
setup.caption: 4. Put all three boxes on the same warm shelf. Score them every day.

flow.do: Show your child the carrot. Say that you will cut it into three equal parts and treat them in three ways. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write them down.
flow.say: This carrot weighs the same however we cut it. One part stays whole. One part is chopped small. One part is grated. Which will rot first? Which will last longest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One carrot, cut three ways. Which rots first? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that one will rot first?
good: It is in the smallest bits.
More of it is open to the air.
There is more for the mould to touch.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is good. Some children guess that the whole carrot will rot first because it is bigger. Write it down and let the test answer it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Cut It Up. You guess before you start.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts the carrot into three equal parts by length. Leave the first whole. Chop the second into cubes about 1 centimetre across. Grate the third. Wet each tissue with a spoon of water and put one in each box. Add one portion to each box and close the lid.
flow.say: A grown-up cuts and grates. Each box gets one damp tissue and one portion. Mark the boxes whole, chopped and grated. Put all three on the same shelf in a warm room.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts the carrot. Put one portion in each box. Mark the boxes. Put them on the shelf.
flow.parent: Cut the carrot into three equal lengths of the same thickness, so the portions have about the same weight. If you have a kitchen scale, weigh each portion. The tissue should be damp, not dripping. Keep the boxes out of direct sun and away from food.

check.q: Why must all three portions start with the same weight?
options: So only the size of the pieces changes
So the carrot looks neat
So the boxes close well
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If one portion were heavier, you would not know if its weight or its size made the difference.

flow.context: In this step, you cut the carrot and set up the three boxes.

flow.do: Every day for six days, look at each box through the lid. Smell is allowed from outside the box only. Give each a score from 0 to 3. Write the scores in the table.
flow.say: Each day, look and score. 0 is no change. 1 is a smell or a soft spot. 2 is slime or a little fuzz. 3 is mostly soft and fuzzy. Do not open the boxes once there is fuzz.
flow.kid: Look at each box every day. Give it a score from 0 to 3.

ask.q: What changed in the grated carrot since yesterday?

flow.parent: Expected: the grated carrot goes first, usually on day 2 or 3, with a smell and slime or white fuzz. The chopped cubes follow a day or two later. The whole piece is slowest and may only soften at the end, or get a bit of fuzz at the cut end. Results vary with the warmth of your room. If nothing changes by day 4, leave the boxes for 3 more days. If all three go together, check that the boxes sit in the same place.
flow.context: In this step, you check the boxes every day and score what you see.

flow.do: On the last day, line the three boxes up. Draw a line graph of the scores for each carrot. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Line up the boxes and look at your graph. Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Line up the boxes. Draw the scores. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the grated carrot had the most surface, so more mould and bacteria could land on it and eat it. After your child has explained, add: this is why earthworms and millipedes help. They chew leaves small, and every bit gives the fungi new surface. When the test is over, a grown-up closes the boxes inside a bag and puts them in the dustbin.
flow.think: Why would a whole carrot in the ground last longer than a grated one?

check.q: The grated carrot rotted first. What is the best reason?
options: Cutting made more surface for decomposers to work on
Grated carrot is heavier
Carrot only rots when it is cut
check.why: Decomposers work on the outside of their food. Grating makes lots of new outside, so there is more room to work. A wrong pick often forgets that all three portions weighed the same.

flow.context: This is the last step of Cut It Up. You draw the graph and explain what you found.

schedule.what: Guess. Cut the carrot. Set up the three boxes.
Look at each box through the lid. Score it from 0 to 3.
Look and score. Draw the graph. Say what you thought, saw and why.

activities.title: Soil Detective: what is in one spoon of soil?

materials.item: soil from a potted plant or from nursery potting soil, 2 spoonfuls
a white plate or a sheet of white paper
a magnifying glass, or a phone camera zoomed in
a toothpick or a pencil, and a spoon
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Spread out the soil. Look for dead bits, threads and tiny animals. Sort what you find into three groups.

activities.record: A drawing of the soil on the plate. Label the dead bits, the white threads, the tiny animals and the bits of rock or sand.
activities.safety: Wash hands after touching soil. Do not put soil near your face.
activities.context: In this activity, you spread out a spoon of soil and look closely for the cleanup crew. You guess what each thing is before you decide.

setup.art: A teaspoon of dark soil spread thinly on a white plate.
setup.caption: 1. Spread one spoon of soil thinly on a white plate.

setup.art: A child looking at soil through a magnifying glass, moving bits apart with a toothpick.
setup.caption: 2. Use a lens and a toothpick to look at the bits.

setup.art: A notebook page with a drawing of soil bits and three labelled groups.
setup.caption: 3. Draw and sort what you find into dead bits, white threads and tiny animals.

flow.do: Spread one spoon of soil on the plate. Ask your child to look without touching and say what they notice. Ask what they wonder.
flow.say: Look at the soil on the plate. What do you notice? What do you wonder? Is anything in it alive?
flow.kid: Look at the soil. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

ask.q: What do you think the dark bits are?
Do you think anything in here is alive?

flow.parent: Do not explain yet. Write down your child's noticing and wondering. Pot soil is fine, and so is soil from a park or a garden.
flow.context: This is the first step of Soil Detective. You notice before you explain.

flow.do: Use the toothpick to move the bits apart. Look with the lens. Find three kinds of things: dead bits of plant, white or grey threads, and tiny animals. Draw each kind you find.
flow.say: Move the bits apart gently. Look for dead plant pieces. Look for fine white threads. Look for any tiny animals. Draw what you find.
flow.kid: Move the soil bits apart. Find dead bits, white threads and tiny animals. Draw them.
flow.parent: You may find pale threads (fungus), small dead leaf pieces, bits of root, and sometimes tiny white or brown animals such as springtails or mites. Pot soil may have few animals. That is normal. A handful of soil from a garden or the base of a tree will have many more. Put the animals back in the soil after looking.

check.q: The white threads in soil are most likely...
options: A fungus growing through the soil
Worm hair
Bits of plastic
check.why: Fungus threads are called hyphae. They are very thin and white or grey, and they grow through the soil and dead leaves. A wrong pick often comes from not looking closely. A hand lens shows that the threads branch.

flow.context: In this step, you look closely for the three kinds of things that are in soil.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what the things they found are doing. Ask which ones are the cleanup crew.
flow.say: Which of the things you found do you think are the cleanup crew? What do you think each one is eating?
flow.kid: Which things are the cleanup crew? What are they eating?
flow.parent: A good answer is that the threads, the tiny animals and the tiny bits of dead plant are all part of the story. The dead plant is the food, and the threads and animals are the eaters. Say that soil is a living thing. A spoon of healthy garden soil has more living beings than there are people in India.
flow.think: If you could look at a spoon of soil from a forest, what would be different?
flow.context: This is the last step of Soil Detective. You think about what each thing does.

activities.title: Marigold Diary: one flower garland, two weeks

materials.item: a used marigold or jasmine garland, or a handful of flowers from the puja shelf
2 small pots or plastic cups with holes, with soil in each
a notebook and pencil
a phone camera, if you like

schedule.what: Bury half of the flowers in one pot and leave half in a dry saucer. Draw both.
Look at both. Draw and write what has changed.
Look at both. Press a stick into the buried flowers.
Dig up the buried flowers. Compare with the dry ones. Explain what happened.

activities.record: A diary page for each day, with a drawing, a short note about colour, smell and softness, and a guess about who has been at work.
activities.safety: Wash hands after touching the soil and the flowers. Do not eat any of the flowers. Anyone with asthma or a mould allergy should not dig up or sniff the fuzzy flowers; a grown-up does it, with gloves.
activities.context: In this activity, you watch a used flower garland change over two weeks. One half goes in damp soil, and one half stays dry.

setup.art: A child pressing marigold flowers into soil in a small pot.
setup.caption: 1. Bury half of the flowers in damp soil in a pot.

setup.art: A saucer of dry marigold flowers on a shelf beside the pot.
setup.caption: 2. Put the other half in a dry saucer on a shelf.

setup.art: A notebook page with two drawings, one of flowers in a pot and one on a saucer, with dates.
setup.caption: 3. Draw both every few days and write what changes.

flow.do: Split the flowers into two heaps. Bury one heap just under the soil in a pot, and sprinkle on a little water. Put the other heap on a dry saucer. Draw both. Ask your child what they think each will look like in two weeks.
flow.say: Half of the flowers go in damp soil. Half stay dry on a saucer. What do you think each will look like in two weeks? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Bury half of the flowers. Keep half dry. What will happen? Why?
flow.parent: Water the buried flowers a little every two or three days, so the soil stays damp. Do not water the dry heap. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Marigold Diary. You set up the two heaps and guess.

flow.do: On day 4 and day 8, look at both heaps. Draw them. Write down the colour, the smell and how soft they feel. On day 8, press a stick into the buried flowers.
flow.say: Look at both heaps. Draw them. Which one has changed more? What do you think is causing the change?
flow.kid: Draw both heaps. Which one changed more? Why?

ask.q: Who do you think has been working on the buried flowers?
good: Tiny living things in the soil.

flow.parent: Expected: the buried flowers turn dark, soft and slimy within a week, and may get white fuzz or a few tiny insects. The dry ones stay papery and keep their shape for weeks. Water makes the difference, as it does for mould on bread. If the buried flowers go sour and slimy, mix in a little dry soil.
flow.context: In this step, you look at the two heaps and draw them.

flow.do: On day 14, dig up the buried flowers. Look at them and compare with the dry heap. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw, and why. Then plant a seed in the pot.
flow.say: Dig up the buried flowers. Compare them with the dry ones. Tell me what you thought, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Dig up the flowers. Compare with the dry ones. Say why.
flow.parent: A strong answer says that decomposers need water, warmth and food, and the damp soil gave them water. Some of the flowers' matter has gone into the air as carbon dioxide and some is in the soil. A seed planted in the pot now grows in what the flowers left.
flow.think: Where did the rest of the flower go?

check.q: The buried flowers rotted and the dry ones did not. What is the best reason?
options: Decomposers need water, and the soil gave them some
Soil is hot
The dry flowers were stronger
check.why: Decomposers need water to dissolve their food. The buried flowers were damp, so the decomposers could work. A wrong pick often forgets that the flowers were the same, and only the water changed.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Marigold Diary. You compare the two heaps and explain.

activities.title: Who Eats It? Follow one meal's leftovers

materials.item: the leftovers of one meal, such as peels, rice, bones, shells, wrappers
a big sheet of paper and a pencil

schedule.what: List the leftovers from one meal. For each, decide who would eat it, and what is left at the end.

activities.record: A table with three columns: the leftover, who or what eats it, and what is left at the end. A last row for things that nobody can eat.
activities.safety: Use only cooked or clean leftovers, never raw meat or raw egg. Wash hands after handling bones, shells and wrappers.
activities.context: In this activity, you look at the leftovers of one meal and work out who would eat each one. Then you find the ones that nobody can eat.

setup.art: A tray with banana peel, rice, a bone, an eggshell, a coconut shell and a plastic wrapper.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the leftovers from one meal on a tray.

setup.art: A big sheet with a three-column table drawn on it.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a table with three columns: leftover, who eats it, what is left.

setup.art: A completed table with two circled rows labelled nobody.
setup.caption: 3. Fill in the table. Circle the leftovers that nobody can eat.

flow.do: Lay out the leftovers of one meal on a tray. Ask your child to name each one. Draw the table on a sheet of paper.
flow.say: These are the leftovers from our meal. Let us name each one. Then we will think about who might eat it.
flow.kid: Name each leftover from our meal. Draw a table.
flow.parent: Use real leftovers from the day's cooking. Include at least one thing that cannot rot, such as a wrapper or a plastic bag, because the later steps need it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Eats It? You list the leftovers.

flow.do: For each leftover, ask your child to guess who would eat it and what would be left at the end. Write it in the table. Use words from this unit: scavenger, detritivore, decomposer.
flow.say: Who would eat this? Is it a scavenger, a detritivore or a decomposer? What would be left at the end?
flow.kid: Who would eat each leftover? What is left at the end?

ask.q: Which leftover is eaten first, and by whom?
good: The rice, by crows and ants.
The peel, by flies and mould.

ask.q: Which leftover takes longest to rot?

flow.parent: Possible answers: peels and rice by ants, flies and then moulds and bacteria. Bones by bacteria and fungi very slowly, over years. Eggshells by bacteria, slowly. Coconut shell by fungi, very slowly. Wrappers and plastic bags: nobody, for hundreds of years.
flow.context: In this step, you work out who the cleanup crew is for each leftover.

flow.do: Count how many leftovers have a crew and how many do not. Ask your child why some have no crew and what could be done about them.
flow.say: How many of our leftovers have a cleanup crew? How many do not? Why do you think that is?
flow.kid: Count the leftovers with a crew. Count the ones with no crew.
flow.parent: Let your child reason it out. The ones with no crew can be reused, repaired or recycled, as in the unit on reduce, reuse and recycle.
flow.think: What could we do with the leftovers that nobody can eat?

check.q: Why does a plastic wrapper last so long?
options: Almost no decomposer makes enzymes that fit plastic
Plastic is too hard to see
Plastic has no weight
check.why: Decomposers have enzymes that fit the materials they have met for millions of years. Plastic is new, so few have the right tool. A wrong pick often confuses not rotting with not being there.

flow.context: This is the last step of Who Eats It? You find the leftovers that nobody can eat.

activities.title: Street Cleaners: ten minutes at a window

materials.item: a window, a balcony or a spot outside the house where food waste is thrown
paper, a pencil and a clock or phone

schedule.what: Watch the same spot for 10 minutes. Count who comes to eat. Sort them into scavengers, detritivores and decomposers.

activities.record: A tally chart of every creature who came to eat, with their name or a drawing, and how many times.
activities.safety: Watch from a window or a safe distance. Never feed or touch street animals, and do not go near a bin or dropped food outdoors.
activities.context: In this activity, you watch one spot for ten minutes and count who comes to clean up the food. You sort them into the crews from this unit.

setup.art: A window view of a street corner with a scatter of vegetable waste and a rubbish bin.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one spot where food or waste lies, such as a rubbish corner or a fallen fruit.

setup.art: A child at a window with a pencil and a tally chart, with crows and a dog in the street.
setup.caption: 2. Watch for ten minutes. Make a tally mark for every creature who comes to eat.

setup.art: A chart with three columns of drawings labelled scavengers, detritivores and decomposers.
setup.caption: 3. Sort the visitors into scavengers, detritivores and decomposers.

flow.do: Choose a spot you can see from a window or a balcony, where food or fruit lies on the ground. Ask your child to guess who will visit in ten minutes.
flow.say: We will watch this spot for ten minutes. Who do you think will come? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Pick a spot. Who will come in ten minutes? Why?
flow.parent: A spot near a rubbish corner, a fallen mango or guava, or the place where leftover rice is put out for the birds works well. If you live high up, watch the bin area from a window. Keep a safe distance from street animals.
flow.context: This is the first step of Street Cleaners. You guess before you watch.

flow.do: Watch for ten minutes. Make a tally mark for every creature who comes to eat. Write down their names or draw them.
flow.say: Make a mark each time a creature comes to eat. Write their name or draw them. Do not forget the tiny ones.
flow.kid: Watch for ten minutes. Make a mark for every creature who eats.

ask.q: Who came first? Who stayed longest?

flow.parent: Crows, kites, mynas, street dogs, cows, ants and flies are typical visitors. Do not get close to street animals. If nothing comes, try again at a different time of day, such as early morning.
flow.context: In this step, you watch the spot and count who comes.

flow.do: Sort every visitor into scavenger, detritivore or neither. Ask your child who is missing from the list and why.
flow.say: Which of your visitors are scavengers? Which are detritivores? Who is not here that you would expect in a forest?
flow.kid: Sort your visitors: scavengers or detritivores. Who is missing?
flow.parent: Crows, kites, dogs and cows are scavengers. Ants are scavengers too. Flies lay eggs, and the grubs are scavengers or detritivores. Moulds on the food are decomposers. Many cities have lost scavengers such as vultures. This is a good moment to tell the vulture story from the how we found out card.
flow.think: If the crows and the dogs all disappeared, what would happen to the street?

check.q: A crow picks at a dropped chapati. What is the crow?
options: A scavenger
A decomposer
A producer
check.why: A scavenger finds and eats leftovers or dead animals. A decomposer digests food outside her body with enzymes, like a fungus. A wrong pick often comes from thinking that every cleanup creature is a decomposer.

flow.context: This is the last step of Street Cleaners. You sort the visitors into the crews.

projects.title: Does rot feed the next plant? Methi in three pots

materials.item: 3 small pots or cups with holes in the bottom
cocopeat, a light brown material sold at nurseries, about 3 cups
vermicompost or well-rotted compost, 3 tablespoons
soil from a healthy potted plant, 1 cup
methi (fenugreek) seeds, about 24
a ruler, a marker and a notebook

schedule.what: Fill the three pots. Plant 8 methi seeds in each. Water them.
Water. Measure the height of each pot's plants. Write it down.
Water. Measure and write the height and colour.
Measure and compare. Draw a bar chart. Explain what you found.

projects.record: A table with the three pots and, for day 4, 8 and 14, the average height of the plants and their colour. A bar chart of height on day 14.
projects.safety: Wash hands after handling soil and compost. Do not eat the seeds or the sprouts from this test.
projects.context: In this project, you grow methi in three different pots over two weeks. It tests whether rotted leaves feed a new plant.

setup.art: Three small pots in a row: one with brown cocopeat, one with dark compost mixed in, and one with garden soil.
setup.caption: 1. Fill pot A with cocopeat only. Fill pot B with cocopeat and 3 spoons of vermicompost. Fill pot C with garden soil.

setup.art: A child pressing methi seeds into the surface of a pot and a small jug of water beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Plant 8 methi seeds in each pot and water them equally.

setup.art: Three pots on a sunny window ledge, labelled A, B and C.
setup.caption: 3. Put the three pots on the same sunny window ledge.

setup.art: A ruler beside a pot of methi seedlings and a notebook with a table.
setup.caption: 4. Measure the plants every few days and write the heights.

flow.do: Show your child the three pots and what goes in each. Ask for a guess and a reason about which pot will grow the best plants.
flow.say: Pot A has only cocopeat. Pot B has cocopeat and rotted compost. Pot C has garden soil. Which pot will grow the best methi? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three pots. Which will grow the best methi? Why?
flow.parent: Cocopeat holds water but has almost no nutrients. Vermicompost is made by worms and microbes from dead plant matter. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Methi project. You guess before you plant.

flow.do: Fill the pots. Plant 8 methi seeds about 1 centimetre deep in each. Water each pot with the same amount, about half a cup. Put all three on the same window ledge.
flow.say: Fill the pots the same way, and plant 8 seeds in each. Water each pot with the same amount. Put them side by side in the light.
flow.kid: Fill the pots. Plant 8 seeds in each. Water all three the same.
flow.parent: Methi seeds sprout in 2 to 4 days. Keep the soil damp, not soaked. The seeds hold their own food for the first week, so the differences between the pots only show clearly after about 10 days. Be patient.

check.q: Why do all three pots get the same amount of seeds, water and light?
options: So only what the seeds grow in is different
So the plants look the same
So the pots do not dry out
check.why: A fair test changes only one thing. If one pot had more light or water, we would not know if the soil or the light made the difference.

flow.context: In this step, you fill and plant the three pots.

flow.do: On days 4 and 8, water the pots equally and measure the height of the plants in each. Write down the colour, too. Look again on day 14.
flow.say: Measure the tallest three plants in each pot. Write the height and the colour. Do all three pots look the same?
flow.kid: Measure the plants in each pot. Write the height and the colour.
flow.parent: Use the average of the three tallest plants. Expected by day 14: pot A is pale or yellowish and short, pot B is tall and deep green, and pot C is in between or similar to B. If all three look the same, the seeds' own food may still be carrying them, so wait a few more days.
flow.context: In this step, you watch the plants and write what you see.

flow.do: On day 14, measure and draw a bar chart of the average heights. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Draw a bar for each pot. Tell me what you thought, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each pot. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the compost holds nutrients from dead leaves and other waste, released by decomposers, and the plants drink them. After they have explained, say that a methi plant has just done what a banana did in the story of the palm.
flow.think: Where did the nutrients in the vermicompost come from, before they were in the compost?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Methi project. You draw the chart and explain what you found.

challenges.title: The Rot Race: make the fastest-rotting jar
challenges.problem: You have 100 grams of fresh vegetable peels, two tablespoons of soil and one jar. Set up the jar so the peels soften and darken as fast as you can in 5 days.
constraints: Use only the peels, the soil, the jar and things from your kitchen: water, a knife, paper and a lid.
No chemicals, no heating, and no adding of ready-made compost.
Change only one thing from your first jar at a time, so you can tell what helped.
After 5 days, score each jar from 0 to 5 for how soft, dark and crumbly the peels are.
materials: 100 grams of fresh vegetable peels (potato, carrot, banana or similar)
a knife (a grown-up cuts), a spoon, water and some dry paper
general: Chop the peels small, because small pieces have more surface for decomposers.
Keep the peels damp, not soaked, because decomposers need water but also air.
Put the jar in a warm place, because decomposers work faster when it is warm.
creative: Mix in shredded dry paper to let in air, and so the jar does not turn slimy.
Open the lid for a minute each day to let in fresh air.
If you have a garden, add a spoon of soil from under a heap of old leaves, so that more decomposers start the work.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your first jar and say why each choice should make the peels rot faster. Set up jar 1. Change one thing, such as the size of the pieces or the warmth, in jar 2. After 5 days, which jar rotted more? Why?
challenges.safety: A grown-up cuts the peels. Open the jars outdoors and do not sniff them. Anyone with asthma or a mould allergy should not open a fuzzy jar. Wash hands after.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about what makes things rot. You use what you learned about size, water, warmth and air to build the fastest-rotting jar.

setup.art: A child drawing a jar design in a notebook with labels for chopped, damp, warm and airy.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch your first jar, and say why each choice should help the peels rot faster.

setup.art: Two jars on a table, one with finely chopped peels and one with big pieces.
setup.caption: 2. Build jar 1. Then build jar 2 with one thing changed.

setup.art: Two jars with a scoring card from 0 to 5 beside them.
setup.caption: 3. After 5 days, score each jar from 0 to 5.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the constraints. Ask your child to sketch a plan for the first jar and say why each choice would help.
flow.say: You want the peels to rot as fast as possible. What do decomposers like? How could you give them more of it? Sketch your plan first.
flow.kid: What do decomposers like? Sketch your jar plan.

ask.q: What would make the decomposers work faster?

flow.parent: Let your child use what they learned from the Cut It Up and Breathing Soil tests. Do not give the answer.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rot Race. You plan before you build.

flow.do: Build jar 1. Chop the peels, mix in the soil, add a little water, and close the lid. Build jar 2 with one change. Put both jars on a warm shelf. Write down what you changed.
flow.say: Build your first jar. Then build a second jar with just one change. Write down what the change is, so we can tell what helped.
flow.kid: Build jar 1. Build jar 2 with one change. Write the change.
flow.parent: Open the jars outdoors, and do not put your nose inside. If a jar goes slimy and sour, add dry paper. Slimy jars have too little air, and sour smells show that different bacteria are at work.
flow.context: In this step, you build the two jars.

flow.do: After 5 days, open the jars and score each from 0 to 5 for how soft, dark and crumbly the peels are. Compare the two jars. Ask which change helped most.
flow.say: Which jar rotted more? What was the one change? Why do you think it helped?
flow.kid: Score both jars. Which rotted more? Which change helped?
flow.parent: Common results: chopping the peels small and adding some dry paper help the most. Too much water makes the jar slimy. A strong answer names the change and the reason. This is a quick version of a compost heap.
flow.think: What would you change next to make the peels rot even faster?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Rot Race. You score the jars and explain.
