quiz.p: A fungus grows through a fallen branch and turns it soft. What is she doing?
opts: Pouring enzymes on the wood and soaking up the food
quiz.why: A fungus digests food outside her body. She pours enzymes on it, and then soaks up what dissolves. A wrong pick often comes from imagining a mouth.

quiz.p: Which pair is a scavenger and a decomposer?
quiz.why: A vulture finds dead animals to eat, so she is a scavenger. Mould digests food with enzymes, so she is a decomposer. Earthworms and millipedes are detritivores.

quiz.p: The limewater above damp soil turned milky. What gas did the soil give out?
quiz.why: Limewater reacts with carbon dioxide and makes tiny white bits of chalk. Soil microbes breathe it out.

quiz.p: In the soil jar test, the jar with only air stayed clear. What does this tell us?
opts: The gas came from the soil and peel, and not from the limewater or air
quiz.why: The check jar shows what happens without the soil. It stayed clear, so the soil and the peel were the cause.

quiz.p: What happens to most of the carbon in a rotting log?
opts: It is breathed out as carbon dioxide
It stays in the log for ever
quiz.why: Decomposers breathe out most of the carbon as carbon dioxide. The rest becomes humus and the bodies of decomposers.

quiz.p: How do plants get the nutrients that were once in dead leaves?
opts: Their roots drink the nutrients that decomposers released into the soil water
quiz.why: Decomposers release the minerals into the soil water, and the roots drink them. Plants do not eat. They make food from air, water and light.

quiz.p: Which is true about matter and energy in a forest?
opts: Matter goes round, and energy flows through and ends as heat
Matter and energy both go round
Energy goes round, and matter is used up
quiz.why: The atoms are used again and again, but energy from the Sun is passed along and ends as heat.

quiz.p: A grated carrot and a whole carrot weigh the same. Why does the grated one rot first?
opts: It has much more surface for decomposers to work on
quiz.why: Grating makes lots of new surface. Decomposers work on surfaces, so there is more room for them.

quiz.p: Which place will keep a dead plant the longest?
opts: A peat bog with no air
quiz.why: Decomposers need air to breathe. In a peat bog, there is almost no air, so dead plants pile up for thousands of years.

quiz.p: What happened to vultures in India in the 1990s and 2000s?
opts: More than 95 out of 100 died after eating cattle treated with diclofenac
quiz.why: Scientists showed that the painkiller diclofenac, left in dead cattle, caused kidney failure in the vultures.

quiz.p: Which of these has no cleanup crew yet?
quiz.why: Plastic is new, so almost no decomposer makes an enzyme that fits it. The peel and the leaf come from plants.

quiz.p: You want to test whether warmth speeds up rotting. Which is a fair test?
opts: Same carrot, same box, one on a warm shelf and one in the fridge
A big carrot on a warm shelf and a small carrot in the fridge
quiz.why: A fair test changes only one thing. Here, only the temperature changes.

items.p: An animal chews dead leaves into small bits. Which crew is she in?
items.why: A detritivore eats bits of dead plants and animals and breaks them smaller. A decomposer digests food outside her body. A scavenger finds dead animals to eat.

items.p: Fungi and bacteria that digest dead things with enzymes are called ____.
items.why: Decomposers pour enzymes on dead matter and soak up the food. Their work turns dead things back into gas and soil.

items.p: A fungus chews her food in a mouth, like an earthworm.
items.why: False. A fungus has no mouth. She pours enzymes on her food, and the enzymes cut it into pieces small enough to soak up.

items.p: Match each living being to the crew she belongs to.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: A vulture finds and eats dead animals. An earthworm and a dung beetle chew dead matter small. A mould digests food outside her body.

items.p: Sort each carrot into whether it rots faster or slower, when the carrots weigh the same.
items: carrot kept cold in the fridge
carrot in a warm, damp box
dry carrot slice on a hot window ledge
items.a: as given
items.why: More cut surface gives decomposers more room to work, and warmth and water help them. A whole, cold or dry carrot gives them less.

items.p: The gas that made the limewater go milky was ____ ____.
items.why: Limewater reacts with carbon dioxide to make tiny white bits of chalk. Soil microbes breathe it out as they eat dead plants.

items.p: In the Breathing Soil test, jar C had only air and limewater. Why was it there?
opts: To show what limewater does with no soil
To make the test look bigger
items.why: A check jar shows what happens without the thing you are testing. Jar C stayed clear, so the gas in the other jar came from the soil.

items.p: Jar B, in the fridge, turned the limewater less milky than jar A in the warm room. Explain why.
items.a: The cold slowed down the decomposers. They breathe out less carbon dioxide when they are cold, so less limewater turned milky.
items.why: A strong answer says that decomposers are living, and cold slows them down. They still eat, but slowly.

items.p: Put these in order, for what happens to a dead leaf on the forest floor.
a: The leaf falls and lies on the ground
A millipede chews the leaf into small bits
Fungi and bacteria digest the bits
Nutrients sink into the soil and a root drinks them
items.why: Detritivores come before decomposers, because they make the surface that the decomposers work on. The nutrients reach a root last.

items.p: When a log rots, most of it goes back into the air as gas.
items.why: True. The carbon is breathed out as carbon dioxide by the decomposers, and much of the rest leaves as water vapour. Only a small part stays as humus.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Earthworm, millipede, termite, mould.
items.a: Mould, because she is a decomposer who digests outside her body. The other three chew dead things small.
items.why: Earthworms, millipedes and termites are detritivores. Mould is a decomposer, who works with enzymes.

items.p: Draw the path of a carbon atom from the air to a leaf, to the soil, and back to the air.
items.a: A circle of arrows: air to leaf, leaf to soil and decomposers, decomposers to air.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the atom returns to the air as carbon dioxide breathed out by decomposers, so the path is a loop.

items.p: Meenakshi's palm log weighs 100 kilograms. About half of a dry log is carbon. How many kilograms of carbon are in the log?
items.why: Half of 100 is 50. As the log rots, much of that carbon is breathed out by decomposers as carbon dioxide.

items.p: Which sentence is true about energy in a food chain?
opts: It goes through once and ends as heat
It goes round and round like carbon
It is used up and disappears
items.why: Energy passes along the chain and leaves as heat. It is not used again. It does not disappear, because the heat spreads out into the air.

items.p: Two friends look at a rotting banana peel on the road.

views.who: Kavya, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: A rotting peel is rubbish. It smells bad, and nobody should touch it.

views.who: Arjun, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: A rotting peel is a meal. Flies, mould and bacteria are eating it, and the rest will feed the soil.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What evidence from this unit supports your choice?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side, says why, and uses a fact such as: the peel is a meal for decomposers, or it can carry germs, so wash hands.
items.why: Both views are true in a way. The peel is a meal for the cleanup crew, and it can carry germs that make people ill. The idea of waste depends on who is looking.

items.p: A 4 centimetre cube is cut into 64 cubes of 1 centimetre. What happens to its surface?
items.why: The big cube has a surface of 96 square centimetres. The 64 small cubes have 384 square centimetres in all. 384 divided by 96 is 4.

items.p: The word for tiny jobs done by tools made by a fungus, to cut food into small pieces, is ____.
items.why: Enzymes are tools made by a living being that cut food into small pieces. A fungus pours them onto her food.

items.p: Rotting and burning make the same gas, carbon dioxide.
items.why: True. Both join carbon from a plant with oxygen. Burning is fast and hot, and rotting is slow and cool.

items.p: Why do earthworms and millipedes speed up rotting?
opts: They make small bits, so fungi have more surface to work on
They add water to the leaf
items.why: Chewing makes many small bits, and each bit has surface that decomposers can use. A wrong pick often comes from thinking that the animals do all the work.

items.p: Match each place to what happens to a dead leaf there.
pairs: Piles up for thousands of years
Dries out and lasts for decades
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Decomposers need warmth, water and air. When one is missing, they work slowly or not at all.

items.p: Sort each of these into whether it goes round in a cycle or flows through and ends.
cats: Flows through and ends as heat
items: Flows through and ends as heat
the energy in a goat's food
Flows through and ends as heat
items.a: as given
items.why: Atoms and water are used again and again. Energy is not used again after it has become heat.

items.p: Many rainforests have poor soil but huge trees. Use the idea of fast nutrient cycling to explain how.
items.a: Fallen leaves rot very fast in the warm, wet air. The nutrients go straight back into the roots of the trees. Most of the nutrients are held in the living trees, so the soil looks poor.
items.why: A strong answer says that the nutrients are in the trees and the leaf litter, not in the soil, and that decomposers return them quickly.

items.p: In the 1960s Australia had a problem with cattle dung. What was the main reason?
opts: Local dung beetles could not use cattle dung
items.why: The local beetles were fitted to the dry pellets of kangaroos. The dung dried into hard pads. Dung beetles from Africa and Europe were brought in to bury it.

items.p: Put these in the order they happened, in the story of the Indian vultures.
a: Vultures cleared dead cattle in a few hours
Cattle were given the painkiller diclofenac
Vultures that ate the cattle died of kidney failure
India banned diclofenac for cattle in 2006
items.why: The vultures were not killed by a disease, but by the drug in the cattle they ate. The ban was the final step.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Glass bottle, plastic bag, banana peel, steel spoon.
items.a: Banana peel, because decomposers can eat it. The other three have no cleanup crew.
items.why: A banana peel is made by a plant, so decomposers have the enzymes to digest it. Glass, plastic and steel are not made by living things.

items.p: A scientist counts 500 vultures in a park in the year 1995. In 2005 she counts 20. How many vultures are gone, and how many out of every 100 is that?
items.a: 480 gone, which is 96 out of 100
items.why: 500 take away 20 is 480. 480 out of 500 is the same as 96 out of 100, because 480 divided by 5 is 96.

items.p: Draw two pictures of a rotting log. In the first, show which gas goes up into the air. In the second, show which materials go down into the soil.
items.a: Log with carbon dioxide arrows going up and water vapour. Log with minerals, humus and nutrients going down to a root.
items.why: A strong drawing shows both ways out. The gas goes to the air, and the minerals go to the soil. A plant will take both back.

items.p: Label this picture: a mushroom on a log. Point to the part that is the fruit and the part that is the fungus's main body.
items.a: The mushroom is the fruit above the log. The fungus's main body is the net of threads, called mycelium, inside the log.
items.why: The mushroom is only the part that makes spores. Most of the fungus is the hidden net of threads in the wood.

items.p: A town is deciding what to do about the dead cattle left on its edge.

views.who: Selvi, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: Bury them or burn them, so no animals come and nobody gets ill.

views.who: Imran, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: Leave them for the vultures and other scavengers, because they clean up fast and nothing is wasted.

items.ask: Whose plan would you choose? What would you need to know first?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason, and names something to find out, such as whether the cattle were treated with a drug that is harmful to vultures.
items.why: Both plans have a point. Vultures clear carcasses fast, but only if the meat is safe for them. The diclofenac story shows why.

items.p: A dry log in a desert lasts for decades, but the same log in a rainforest is gone in a few years. What does this show?
opts: Rotting depends on warmth, water and air
items.why: The same kind of wood rots at different speeds depending on whether decomposers have water, warmth and air.

items.p: A farmer cuts her wheat and carries every straw away for years. Her soil gets poorer. Explain why.
items.a: The wheat took nutrients from the soil. When all the straw is carried away, the nutrients never return, because there is nothing left to rot into the soil.
items.why: A strong answer names the nutrients, says they are taken up by plants, and points out that the loop is broken when the plants never rot in the field.

items.p: You want to test if warmth speeds up rotting. Plan a fair test with chopped carrot. Say what you change, what you keep the same, and what you measure.
items.a: Change the temperature, for example a warm shelf and a fridge. Keep the same carrot, the size of the pieces, the box, the water and the days. Measure by scoring softness, smell and fuzz each day.
items.why: A fair test changes one thing. It keeps the rest the same, and it measures the result in the same way each time.

items.p: Jar A has chopped peel in damp soil. Jar B has big chunks of peel in damp soil. Both are warm. What is a fair prediction?
opts: Jar A rots faster because it has more surface
Jar B rots faster because the chunks are bigger
Both rot at the same speed
items.why: Small pieces have more surface. Decomposers work on surfaces, so jar A should go first.

items.p: A tiny dark crumbly soil made from partly rotted plants is called ____.
items.why: Humus is the dark, soft part of soil left when dead plants and animals are partly broken down. It holds water and nutrients.

items.p: If the limewater above a jar of soil stays clear, nothing in the jar is alive.
items.why: False. The jar may be too cold, too dry or too short on food, so the decomposers breathe out too little gas to see. A clear result means that little gas was made, and it does not prove that nothing is alive.

items.p: A compost heap loses half its weight each month. It starts at 160 kilograms. How many kilograms are left after 4 months?
items.why: 160 halves to 80, then 40, then 20, then 10. After 4 months, 10 kilograms are left.

items.p: Kavya says, 'Plastic does not rot because it is too strong.' Explain why this reason is not right.
items.a: Strength is not the reason. Decomposers have enzymes that fit plant and animal matter. Plastic is a new material, and almost no decomposer has an enzyme for it yet.
items.why: A strong answer says that rotting depends on enzymes that fit the material, not on how strong or hard it is.

items.p: Why does a compost heap feel warm in the middle?
opts: Decomposers give out heat as they breathe
Water in the heap is boiling
items.why: Respiration gives out heat. Millions of tiny decomposers working together warm the heap, and the heat comes from the stored energy of the plants.

items.p: Match each way of speeding up rotting to its reason.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each trick gives decomposers more of what they need: surface, water, warmth or air.

items.p: Some scientists think the rise of fungi that digest wood ended the age of coal.

views.who: A scientist who supports the idea (imagined)
views.says: Coal stopped forming when fungi learned to digest lignin, the toughest part of wood.
Coal also stopped forming because of changes in climate and in the shape of the continents.

items.ask: Which view is stronger? What evidence would help you decide?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer says what evidence is missing, such as the dates for when the fungi appeared, or what the climate was like at the time.
items.why: This is an open question. The first idea is plausible but has not been proved, and good scientists test it.

items.p: Draw a loop for carbon: the air, a leaf, a goat and a fungus. Then draw a straight arrow for energy that starts at the Sun and ends as heat.
items.a: A circle for carbon through air, leaf, goat, fungus and back to air. A straight line from the Sun to heat.
items.why: The loop shows that matter goes round, and the straight line shows that energy flows through. Both are needed to explain how life carries on.

items.p: What does it mean to say that a forest has no waste?
opts: Every leftover is food for something
Nothing ever dies in a forest
items.why: A forest recycles because decomposers eat the leftovers and send the matter back to plants. A wrong pick often mixes up clean with recycled.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Rotting, burning, breathing, melting.
items.a: Melting, because it does not join carbon with oxygen to make carbon dioxide. The other three do.
items.why: Rotting, burning and breathing are all respiration or burning, which turn food or fuel and oxygen into carbon dioxide and energy. Melting is only a change of state.

items.p: A rainforest is cleared and the soil quickly turns poor. Use the idea of the nutrient cycle to explain what went wrong.
items.a: In a rainforest, most of the nutrients are in the living trees and the leaf litter. When the trees are cut and carried away, the nutrients go with them. Heavy rain then washes away what is left, and the soil cannot feed new plants.
items.why: A strong answer says that the cycle was broken. The nutrients were held in the trees, and the cutting took them away.

items.p: A scientist finds that dead leaves in a cold forest last for years. Which is the best explanation?
opts: Cold slows decomposers, so they eat slowly
items.why: Decomposers are living, and cold slows them. The same kind of leaf rots in months in a warm forest.

items.p: Energy that has become ____ spreads out into the air and cannot be used again by living things.
items.why: Heat is energy spread out into the surroundings. Living things cannot use it again, so energy must keep coming from the Sun.

open_questions.q: Which microbes could one day digest plastic, and could they do it fast enough to matter?
open_questions.why_open: A few microbes with enzymes that cut one kind of plastic have been found. Nobody yet knows if they can be used on the scale of the world's waste.

open_questions.q: How much do underground fungus networks really share between trees?
open_questions.why_open: Some studies find sugars and signals moving between trees, and others find little. Scientists are still testing how common and how important it is.

open_questions.q: Did the rise of wood-digesting fungi end the age of coal?
open_questions.why_open: The dates fit, but changes in climate and the shape of the continents could also be causes. It has not been settled.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of decomposers live in one spoon of soil?
open_questions.why_open: Most soil microbes have never been grown in a lab. Scientists estimate there are thousands of kinds in a spoon, but the count is still changing.

open_questions.q: How much did the loss of vultures raise rabies in India?
open_questions.why_open: Some studies estimate a large effect, but dog numbers and rabies depend on many things. It is hard to separate the vultures' part.

open_questions.q: Will more of the carbon in soil be breathed out as the world warms?
open_questions.why_open: Warmer soil makes decomposers faster, which could release more carbon dioxide. Scientists are still measuring how large this effect will be.

maths.problem: A carrot cube is 4 centimetres on each side. It has 6 faces. Each face is 4 times 4 square centimetres. How many square centimetres is the surface of the whole cube?
maths.explain: Each face is 4 times 4, which is 16 square centimetres. The cube has 6 faces. 6 times 16 is 96.
maths.why_maths: The surface is what decomposers work on, so you need to be able to work it out before you compare big pieces with small ones.

maths.problem: The same cube is cut into 64 small cubes, each 1 centimetre on each side. Each small cube has a surface of 6 square centimetres. How many square centimetres is the surface of all 64 small cubes together? How many times bigger than the big cube's surface is that?
maths.answer: 384 square centimetres, which is 4 times bigger.
maths.explain: 64 times 6 is 384. The big cube had 96. 384 divided by 96 is 4. So the same carrot has 4 times as much surface when it is cut small.
maths.context: In the Cut It Up test, you cut a carrot into three kinds of pieces and see which rots first.
maths.why_maths: The maths shows why a chopped carrot rots faster. The decomposers have more outside to work on, with the same weight of carrot.

maths.problem: In the Cut It Up test, the grated carrot scored 3 on day 3. The chopped carrot scored 3 on day 5. The whole carrot scored 3 on day 9. How many times longer did the whole carrot take than the grated one? How many days longer?
maths.answer: 3 times longer, which is 6 days longer.
maths.explain: 9 divided by 3 is 3, so 3 times as long. 9 take away 3 is 6, so 6 days longer. These are made-up numbers, and yours will differ.
maths.context: In the Cut It Up test, you score three kinds of carrot every day for six days. Here are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Comparing how long each took shows how much cutting speeds up rotting, in a way that you can tell to a friend.

maths.problem: A pile of leaf litter weighs 80 grams. Every month, half of what is left is eaten. How many grams are left after 3 months? After how many months is less than 10 grams left?
maths.answer: 10 grams after 3 months. Less than 10 grams after 4 months.
maths.explain: 80 halves to 40, then 20, then 10. After 3 months, 10 grams are left. Half of 10 is 5, so after 4 months less than 10 grams are left.
maths.why_maths: Rotting often removes a fixed share each month, and halving again and again is how you can predict how long a pile will last.

maths.problem: A scientist counts 1000 vultures in a district. Ten years later she counts 30. How many have gone? How many out of every 100 is that? These are made-up numbers.
maths.answer: 970 have gone, which is 97 out of every 100.
maths.explain: 1000 take away 30 is 970. 970 out of 1000 is the same as 97 out of 100, because 970 divided by 10 is 97.
maths.why_maths: A count of 970 is hard to picture. 97 out of every 100 shows how large the fall was.

maths.problem: A dry log has a mass of 100 kilograms. About half of it is carbon. A fungus breathes out 3 kilograms of that carbon in the first year. How many kilograms of carbon are left in the log? What fraction of the carbon is that?
maths.answer: 47 kilograms are left, and 3 out of 50 has gone.
maths.explain: Half of 100 is 50 kilograms of carbon. 50 take away 3 is 47. 3 out of 50 is the fraction that has gone, which is 6 out of 100.
maths.why_maths: Following the carbon from year to year shows how slowly a big log is used up, compared to a leaf.

maths.problem: Three jars of limewater, A, B and C, are checked at the same time. Jar A turns milky in 1 day. Jar B turns milky in 3 days. Jar C never does. Put the jars in order, from the most gas to the least gas, and say what the order tells you.
maths.answer: A, then B, then C. Jar A has the busiest decomposers, and jar C has none.
maths.explain: The quicker the limewater turns milky, the faster the gas is made. Jar A made it fastest, jar B slower, and jar C none. So jar A's soil is the busiest, and jar C is the check.
maths.context: In the Breathing Soil test, you set up three jars and watch how fast the limewater turns milky. Here are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Putting results in order is how you see which jar gave out the most gas, and what that says about the soil.

maths.problem: A methi plant in pot A is 4 centimetres tall after 14 days. The plants in pot B with compost are 11 centimetres tall. How many times taller are the plants in pot B? What does this suggest? These numbers are made up.
maths.answer: A bit less than 3 times taller (11 divided by 4 is about 2.75). It suggests that the compost fed the plants.
maths.explain: 11 divided by 4 is 2 with 3 left over, so about 2.75. Three times would be 12, so it is a bit less. The extra growth is a hint that the compost nutrients helped, though one test is not proof.
maths.context: In the Methi project, you grow methi in cocopeat, cocopeat with compost, and garden soil. Here are made-up heights.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one height by another tells you how many times bigger, so you can compare the pots with a single number.

roots.context: We have followed a dead log into the air and the soil. Now we ask what the cleanup crews tell us about waste, and about what we are made of.

deep_truth.truth: The soil in the jar breathed out carbon dioxide, and the limewater above it went milky. Tiny decomposers eat dead leaf and turn it into gas and into food for plants. In a forest, every leftover is someone's meal. 'Waste' is only what nobody has learned to eat yet.
deep_truth.habit: We split the world into useful things and waste, as if some things were made to be thrown away. A dead leaf, a dropped peel and a fallen palm look like rubbish. They are food for the next being, and the split only appears where there is no one to eat what is left.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Breathing Soil test, the jar with soil and peel turned limewater milky, and the jar with only air did not. In Cut It Up, the finely grated carrot was eaten first. Plastic stays because few decomposers have the enzymes for it.

three.who_am_i: The carbon in your body was in the air, in plants and in other animals before it was in you, and it will move on again.
three.what_is_life: Life is made of eating and being eaten. A fungus is as much a part of life as a lion, and she is the one who sends the atoms back for the next plant.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is a loop of matter powered by the Sun. Every leaf has been in the soil, the air and a body many times already.

roots.thread: A leaf is air and water made into a body by sunlight. When the leaf dies, a fungus or a worm unmakes it, and the same atoms go back into the air and the soil. A new leaf then makes the atoms into a body again. No part of the loop is the real beginning, and nothing in it is waste. Each body is a place where the same atoms rest for a while. The thing that keeps the loop going is the Sun, whose energy is passed along and ends as heat.

teachings.teaching: From food, living beings come into being. Food comes from rain, and rain comes from giving and sharing.
teachings.link: The verse names a loop of food, rain and living beings. The soil jar shows part of that loop, where dead food turns back into the gas and minerals that plants use.

teachings.teaching: All things grow and flourish, and then each returns to its root. Returning to the root is called stillness.
teachings.link: A leaf grows from the soil and the air, and returns to them. The cycle is a return to the root.

teachings.teaching: From dust you were made, and to dust you will return.
teachings.link: Many traditions say it in their own words. The science says it as a count of atoms: the carbon and the minerals in a body come from the soil and the air, and they go back.

science.text: Matter is not made or lost when things rot. The atoms of carbon, nitrogen and the other elements are only moved from body to body, to the soil and the air.
Underground networks of fungus threads may carry sugars and signals between trees. Scientists still argue about how common this is and how much it matters for a forest.

other_view.who: The Charvaka school of ancient India
other_view.view: A person is only matter in a certain arrangement, and when the arrangement falls apart nothing remains. The body goes back to the elements, and there is nothing more to say. A view rooted in oneness can sit with this: it agrees on the atoms, and asks whether anything else is going round besides the atoms.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. Breathing Soil: the limewater turns milky when carbon dioxide arrives. Jar A (warm soil and fresh peel) usually turns the limewater cloudy within a day in an Indian kitchen, jar B in the fridge is slower and weaker, and jar C stays clear or gets only a faint skin. How fast and how strong depends on the soil and the warmth, so the steps say what to do if jar A stays clear (more peel, a little water, a warmer spot, wait one more day) and how to check the limewater with a breath first. Chuna is a caustic lime, so the limewater steps are marked for a grown-up. Cut It Up: grated carrot usually goes soft, sour-smelling and slimy in two to three days in a warm room, chopped cubes follow, and the whole piece lasts longest. The scores are rough, so the table asks for the same judge every day. Methi project: the differences between the three pots show only after about ten days, because the seeds carry their own food at first. The timings assume a child who needs a grown-up for cutting. Two details to check before the unit goes live: the size of the Oregon fungus (about nine to ten square kilometres in the usual accounts) and the figure that more than 95 out of 100 vultures of three kinds were lost, which is the usual summary of the published counts. The videos have no address yet.

how_we_found_out.story: In the 1990s, bird watchers in India noticed that vultures were vanishing. Vultures had always cleared the bodies of dead cattle and wild animals. At Keoladeo National Park in Rajasthan, Vibhu Prakash of the Bombay Natural History Society counted nests each year, and the numbers kept falling. By the early 2000s, more than 95 of every 100 vultures of three kinds were gone. Many scientists first thought an infectious disease was spreading from bird to bird. Then Lindsay Oaks and his team tested dead vultures in Pakistan. The birds' kidneys had failed, and they had eaten cattle treated with a painkiller called diclofenac. Their paper in Nature in 2004 showed that the drug was the cause. India banned diclofenac for cattle in 2006.
how_we_found_out.who: Vibhu Prakash, Lindsay Oaks, Rhys Green and many other scientists in India, Pakistan and Britain
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People first thought that an infectious disease was killing the vultures. The team showed that the birds were being poisoned by a painkiller in the dead cattle they ate, and that a vulture's kidneys fail within days of eating it.
